FOREWORD This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards on 15 January 1989, after the draft finalized by the Alcohols and Allied Products Sectional Committee had been approved by the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products Division Council. There are diverse methods for determining the ethanol content of alcoholic liquids and their preparations. These methods are based on the density, refractive index, oxidation index, gas chromatographic retention time, etc. The simplest and the most widely used method is the one based on the density of ethanol-water mixtures, which decreases with the increase of ethanol content in a manner which has been determined to the highest degree of accuracy. The density data on alcohol-water mixtures as a function of temperature made available by OIML (Qrganisation Internationale de Metrologie LegalelInternationai Organization of Legal Metrology) is of the ultimate accuracy available to date and is a cohaborative work based on calculations ( by computer ) on the results of measurements made by U. S. National Bureau of Standards; National Bureau of Quality and Measures, Poland; National Research Laboratory of Metrology, Japan; Montpellier Faculty of Pharmacy, France; Physikalisch Technische Bundesanstalt, F. R. Germany; and the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry. The OIML data in sofaras ethanol content by volume is concerned, uses 20�C as reference temperature, that is, real strength by volume defined as volume of ethanol at 20�C in 100 volumes of the alcoholic sample at 20�C. The hydrometer tables derived from OIML data, for example, the French tables, `Guide Pratique D'Alcoometrie, 1980', published by Librairie Administrative, P. Qudin, 86000 Poitiers ( France ), though using hydrometers standardized at 20�C are accurately valid from the lowest - 10�C to the highest + 40�C ambient temperatures. Computation of alcohol strength of aqueous-alcoholic solutions could be done by pyknometry or hydrometry. For pyknometry the directly usable tables of apparent specific gravity to/to in the range of Indian ambient temperatures 10 to 40�C based on OlML data are available in IS 3506: 1989 bTables for alcoholometry ( by pyknometer method ) ($rst revision )`. For hydrometry, the present standard is being revised as this was based on earliar French tables `Guide Pratique D'Alcoometrie 1950', which have now been superseded by OIML data and consequent revision of French hydrometer tables of 1980. The present hydrometer tables will enable us to achieve the ultimate OIML accuracy and eventually to fall in line with the international practice of computation of alcoholic content adopting 20�C as reference temperature. In the meantime, while the alcoholic content in the country is required to be computed at 15�C ( medicinal and toilet preparations ) or at 15~56�C ( Indian-made foreign liquors, rectified spirit, etc ) the results or values of ethanol content at the internationally adopted 20�C as given in Table 1 can readily be converted to our present requirements by applying the minor corrections as given in Table 2. Table 1 has been drawn up on the basis of information and data available in `Guide Pratique D'Alcoometrie, 1980' and OIML Tables, pp. 29-41, `<Table II : p = p ( q, t )" where q = ethanolic content by volume at 20�C and t the ambient temperature. Table 1 is primarily alcohol-richness table ( ethanol content at 20"/t" ) while the volume conversion factor incorporated therein will enable the real strength ( 20"/20" ) to be readily evaluated. Also, the volume conversion factor to convert kilograms to litres for a given observed degree of the alcoholic solution is also incorporated in the same table. Thus Table 1 is a single table incorporating such data as was provided in the two separate tables in the earlier version of the standard plus the provision to evaluate Table 2 of this standard is the same as * the real strength, which the earlier table did not provide. Table 2 of IS 3506 : 1989 and it has been computed from OIML data. In reporting the result of a test made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values ( revised )`.

1 SCOPE 1.1 This standard covers method of obtaining volumetric content of ethanol at 20�C (Table 1 ) and at 15�C and 15*56"C( Table 2) in an alcoholic solution ( ethanol-water ) using the centesimal hydrometers calibrated at 20�C.
1.1.1 Table 1 gives alcohol-richness data, that is, ethanol content by volume at 20�C in the sample at t"C against the observed ( hydrometer ) degree at 0.1 degree interval at the observed temperature, t"C in the range 0' to 40�C. The volume conversion factor given in this table enables computation of real strength (20"/20" ). Also, the volume in litres per 100 kg ( in air ) of the sample at the observed degree is also incorporated in the same table. Table 2 gives the minor corrections for converting the real strength at the international reference temperature to that at 15.56"C or 15�C for use in the country until the adoption of international reference temperature 20�C for excise purposes.
NOTE -The volume in litres per 100 kg (in air) of the alcohol-water sample at the observed degree is computed from the OIML data, giving volume corresponding to 100 kg in vacuum, and applying the correction for buoyancy, p in air, given by p = mass xair density x (reciprocal density of samplereciprocal d&sity of-weights used). For m&s = 100 ke. air densitv at 27�C = 0.001 177 e/cm3 and the d&ity of cast-iron weights as 7.3 g/en? we have p = 0.102 to 0.133 kg from alcohol strength 0 to 100 Dercent. The observed volume shall be expressed in litres at the particular temperature, for example, 1 025.3 litres at 25�C. 3.3 Ethanol Content by Volume of an AlcoholWater Mixture at to C This is also called Alcohol-Richness, that is, the number of parts by volume of ethanol at 20�C contained in 100 parts by volume of.the mixture at VT. position. Do not allow the portion of the stem which stands above the liquid surface to be welted as far as possible as otherwise the total mass of the hydrometer will be increased and the result will bz vitiated. For correct reading, the stem shall not be wetted more than a few millimetres above the liquid surface. Care shall also be taken that no portion of the hydrometer comes into contact with sides of the glass cylinder or the thermometer. Keep the eye in level with the surface of the liquid and take the reading of the hydrometer and the thermometer. 6.3 The temperature shall be recorded to the nearest 0.5'C above the surface of the mercury when it stands between any two consecutive divisions of the thermometer and the hydrometer reading to the nearest division below the surface of the sample.
NOTE - Generallv, the observed volume is determined before taking the hydrometer reading. Since this observed volume is referred to a particular temperature ( the temperature of the liquid ), it is obvious that this temperature shall not change when taking the hydrometer reading. It is, however, possible that the glass cylinder may have a temperature different from chat of the liquid. Therefore, the inside of glass cylinder shall be washed first with the liquid itself. Care, however, shall be taken not to wet the outside of glass cylinder because, due to the evaporation of alcchol, heat will be lost.

4 CENTESIMAL HYDROMETERS 4.1 Hydrometers shall be graduated in nominal ranges 0 to 5 percent volume . . . . . . 95 to 100 percent vclume or 0 to 10 percent volume . . . . . . 90 to 100 percent volume at 0.1 percent volume sub-divisions. An additional hydrometer may be used to cover the nominal range 98 to 103 percent volume or 93 to 103 percent volume ( the figures of imaginary alcohol content more than 100 percent are necessary for adjustment of hydrometers in highly concentrated alcoholwater mixturFs at temperatures between 20 and 40�C. the density of which formally corresponds to alcohol content more than 100 percent ). The hydrometers may or may not incorporate a thermometer. In the latter case, aseparate thermometer shall be used. The hydrometers shall, in general, conform to the specifications as laid down in IS 3608. These alcoholometers could be fabricated indigenously. 4.1.1 The hydrometers shall be used to determine the ethanol content of only simple spirits, that is, mixtures of ethanol and water. The hydrometers shall be kept clean. Before using the hydrometer, it shall be washed with the alcoholic solution to be tested. 5 THERMOMETERS 5.1 Thermometers having the range 50�C with sub-divisions at every 0-W used.
